correctness.rationale: For each maximal clique, an unselected vertex cannot have two selected clique neighbors, so its selected intersection is empty, singleton, or full. The vertex/block incidence graph is a tree. The exact boundary states selected, unselected-with-zero-descendant-neighbors and unselected-with-one-descendant-neighbor form an exhaustive disjoint partition. The algebraic block transitions and vertex convolution handle uniquely all selected-neighbor contributions; induction yields the full multivariate enumerator. There are O(n) block incidences and constant-gate updates per incidence; the standard block decomposition costs O(n+m). Direct brute-force subset enumeration agrees coefficientwise for all 1816 generated instances of order up to 12 in verify.py, including singleton/complete graphs and different clique articulation arrangements. Finiteness of the experiment is stated and does not replace the general proof.

broader_coverage.reasoning: The new theorem covers all connected block graphs, including graphs with triangles, arbitrarily many overlapping clique blocks and unbounded clique number. Neither the tree-domain theorem nor the threshold-domain theorem nor generic exponential algorithms logically entail the claimed linear-size weighted circuit. A generic junction-tree approach might supply an equivalent result elsewhere; that is retained as residual risk.

originality.rationale: In the inspected 2026 primary research study of exactly this P3-convex-set counting problem, the proved linear algorithms address trees (Theorem 3) and threshold graphs (Theorem 14); the general method remains exponential. Its Section 4.3.1 already identifies the none/one/all clique restriction, so this elementary local observation is credited. It does not give the arbitrary-block-clique incidence-tree recursion or the linear-size multivariate circuit. Other compared research records concern different invariants or graph domains. value.rationale: The motivating 2026 paper proves #P-hardness already on split graphs and supplies tractable tree/threshold cases, so a substantial additional tractable family is a natural structural counting target. Connected block graphs admit unbounded clique sizes and arbitrary clique-block incidence trees, and the theorem handles every weighted vertex subset simultaneously in a compact arithmetic circuit. The incidence arrangement affects actual coefficients (e.g. three triangles in a chain vs three sharing a vertex), showing the theorem is more than a routine block-size product. The result is mathematically motivated, structurally exact and algorithmically useful without invoking an unproved downstream conjecture.
